prompt: Of 55,800 sessions, 8,062 paid. What is the conversion from landing, in per cent, to one decimal place?
Which rate isolates one step of a funnel, so a problem there can be found?

choices.text: Conversion from landing, since it is the number that is reported to the board each month
choices.why: It accumulates every step above, so it hides where the loss is.

choices.text: Conversion from the previous step
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The count reaching the last step
choices.why: A count with nothing to compare it to.

choices.text: Sessions per visitor
choices.why: That describes return visits, not a step.

prompt: Only 55% of sessions go from the menu to choosing a box, the steepest step. Why is it probably not the step to fix?

choices.text: Browsing is normal
choices.why: Right. A steep step can be doing its job.

choices.text: It is the same on both devices, so it must be measured wrongly, since real steps always differ
choices.why: Being the same on both devices is a sign it is normal, not wrong.

choices.text: Fixing it would cost too much
choices.why: Cost is not the reason given; nothing shows it is broken.

choices.text: It comes before checkout
choices.why: Position does not decide what is broken.

prompt: How does the lesson find the step that is broken rather than steep?

choices.text: By picking the step with the lowest rate
choices.why: That finds the steep one.

choices.text: By asking customers
choices.why: Useful for why, not the method used here to find where.

choices.text: By running an A/B test on every one of the steps of the funnel at once
choices.why: A test comes after a step has been found.

choices.text: By comparing devices
choices.why: Right. Desktop and mobile differ at one step only.

prompt: What share of mobile sessions that reached checkout paid, in per cent?
14.4% of sessions paid and 27.0% of visitors paid. Which is right?

choices.text: Sessions, because they are the raw data
choices.why: Visitors are computed from the same data.

choices.text: Visitors, because people matter more than visits, and a session is a technical detail of the site
choices.why: A form is judged per visit; neither is wrong.

choices.text: Both; they count different things
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Neither
choices.why: Both are correct counts.

prompt: Which funnel is the right lens for judging a checkout form?

choices.text: The person funnel
choices.why: It mixes in people who failed and came back later.

choices.text: The session funnel
choices.why: Right. The form fails per visit.

choices.text: Neither; forms are judged by complaints
choices.why: Complaints help with why, not with how much.

choices.text: The landing page funnel
choices.why: Checkout is at the other end.

prompt: A person funnel counts a visitor as converted if they paid within 30 days. Why does its latest month look worse than earlier ones?

choices.text: Recent visitors have not yet had their thirty days, so some of their payments are still to come
choices.why: Right. Censoring again.

choices.text: The site got worse
choices.why: Possible, but the window explains it without anything changing.

choices.text: Visitors are counted twice in the latest month, once in each of their sessions there
choices.why: A person funnel counts each visitor once.

choices.text: Holidays
choices.why: No holiday is needed to explain it.

prompt: A visitor fails at mobile checkout and pays on a laptop an hour later. In a cookie-based person funnel, what are they?

choices.text: One converted person
choices.why: The cookie sees two browsers.

choices.text: Excluded
choices.why: Nothing excludes them.

choices.text: One failed person
choices.why: The laptop payment is counted too.

choices.text: Two people, one failed and one converted
choices.why: Right, which undercounts exactly the people a broken mobile form produces.

prompt: If 9,242 mobile sessions at checkout paid at the desktop rate of 82.8%, about how many would pay? Answer to the nearest whole number.
Why is '3,185 more paid sessions a month' a ceiling rather than a forecast?

choices.text: March is a short month
choices.why: March has 31 days.

choices.text: The figure is in orders, not sessions
choices.why: It is in sessions, which is a second caution.

choices.text: Phones may never match laptops at payment
choices.why: Right. Say 'up to'.

choices.text: Desktop's rate is going to fall once mobile is fixed, since the two share one checkout page
choices.why: Nothing suggests desktop would change.

prompt: The team redesigns mobile checkout and compares the funnel of the month before with the month after. What is wrong?

choices.text: Funnels cannot be compared
choices.why: They can; a before-and-after just cannot isolate the change.

choices.text: It is a before-and-after, with everything else that changed mixed in
choices.why: Right. An A/B test isolates the change.

choices.text: One month is too short for a funnel
choices.why: Length is not the flaw.

choices.text: The redesign must be tested on desktop first
choices.why: Desktop is not the broken step.

prompt: A funnel shows where people stop. Which question can it not answer by itself?

choices.text: Why they stop
choices.why: Right. That needs search terms, error logs and asking customers.

choices.text: How many reached checkout
choices.why: That is exactly what it counts.

choices.text: Which step loses the most sessions
choices.why: It answers that directly.

choices.text: How desktop compares with mobile at each step of the journey
choices.why: Splitting by device answers it.
